newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Investors await action on privatisation in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Investors await action on privatisation in Bosnia.

text.p: Bosnia could lose out on potential foreign investment by failing to adopt privatisation laws which have languished in the Moslem-Croat federation parliament for months, foreign experts said on Thursday.
"We've been expecting these laws to be passed since November at every parliament meeting but adoption kept getting postponed," said Christine Szuszkiewicz, spokeswoman for a U.S.consulting firm.

A team of federation and foreign experts have prepared drafts of six laws regulating the privatisation of companies, banks and housing and the restitution of property confiscated by former communist authorities.
The federation cabinet approved the drafts without significant objections but the parliament, preoccupied with other political disputes, has dragged its feet.
"There are a number of business laws in practice, but they do not really clearly define investors' rights, like lawsuits and protection from corruption," Szuszkiewicz told Reuters.
"And certainly it (delay in privatisation) does postpone investors' further interest because they cannot buy a company unless it is privatised."
The World Bank has warned that the federation would be judged by investors on how quickly it pushes through privatisation.

"The federation has started off well with its programme of privatisation but all further delays, all reversible acts are going to minimise the credibility of the government in the eyes of investors," the World Bank wrote in a recent study.
Bosnia's 3-1/2 year war ended with a U.S-brokered peace accord in December 1995, which opened the way for the revival of a seriously damaged economy.

While reconstruction efforts, for which the international community pledged $5.1 billion over four years, have started to repair the country's infrastructure, foreign investors have been hesitant to enter Bosnia in the first year and a half of peace.

Szuszkiewicz said she was hopeful the next parliament session, set for May 6, would tackle the law on sales of publicly-owned apartments. The parliament should debate other privatisation laws at subsequesnt sessions.

Once the laws are passed, "small-scale privatisation" of companies with under 50 employees and assets valued at less than 500,000 German marks ($290,000) should take effect quickly, Szuszkiewicz said.
The country's two entities -- the federation and the Serb republic -- have been working on separate privatisation legislation.
Serb and federation officials will have to harmonise laws governing restitution of property and the criteria for privatising major socialist-era enterprises with assets in both entities.
